about: The zakat screen's explainer statements (all-in-one spec 5.1, 6). A note is 'source-checked' when every statement in it was located in the fetched Arabic of the school primers (or, where a primer is silent, a named work of the same school) and cross-located in Bidayat al-Mujtahid; the located Arabic is stored in evidence[].quote. Notes that rest on modern figures or on a single witness stay 'draft'. Nothing here is scholar-reviewed. No hadith number or page is stated.

notes.text: In all four schools, zakat on cash, gold, silver and goods for sale is one fortieth (2.5%) of their value, once a full lunar year has passed over wealth that reaches nisab. The fortieth on gold and silver is agreed. Ibn Rushd records that the Zahiri school holds no zakat is due on goods for sale.
notes.sourceLead: Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Book of Zakat, reporting agreement on one fortieth for gold and silver, and the difference over goods for sale; Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ijma', Book of Zakat; the four schools' primers, Book of Zakat

evidence.place: Book of Zakat, section on gold and silver
evidence.quote: فإنهم اتفقوا على أن الواجب في ذلك هو ربع العشر: أعني في الفضة والذهب معا

evidence.place: Book of Zakat, on goods for sale
evidence.quote: فذهب فقهاء الأمصار إلى وجوب ذلك، ومنع ذلك أهل الظاهر

notes.text: In all four schools, nisab, the least wealth on which zakat is due, is twenty mithqal (dinars) of gold or two hundred dirhams of silver. The silver figure is agreed. For gold, Ibn Rushd records scholars outside the four schools who set it differently, al-Hasan al-Basri among them.
notes.sourceLead: Hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri on five awaq of silver, in al-Bukhari and Muslim, Book of Zakat. For gold, the report from Ali in Abu Dawud, Book of Zakat; Ibn Rushd notes that nothing is established from the Prophet ﷺ for gold as it is for silver. Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ijma', Book of Zakat; Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Book of Zakat

evidence.place: Book of Zakat
evidence.quote: وانفرد الحسن البصري، فقال: ليس فيما دون أربعين دينارا صدقة

notes.text: Turning dinars and dirhams into grams depends on how much a dinar and a dirham are reckoned to weigh. This calculator offers two sets of figures.

positions.by: A dinar of 4.25 g and a dirham of 2.975 g
positions.text: 85 g of gold and 595 g of silver. Ibn 'Uthaymin gives these figures.

positions.by: 7.5 tola of gold and 52.5 tola of silver
positions.text: 87.48 g of gold and 612.36 g of silver, which makes a tola 11.664 g. Darul Ifta Birmingham, a Hanafi fatwa council, gives these figures.

notes.sourceLead: Al-Durar al-Saniyya fiqh encyclopedia, on the nisab of gold and silver in grams, quoting Ibn 'Uthaymin; Darul Ifta Birmingham, answer on the nisab threshold for gold, for the tola figures

notes.text: Cash and goods for sale have no nisab of their own, so they are measured against gold or silver. Scholars today differ on which to use, and the two can be far apart.

positions.text: The Hanafi primer values goods for sale by whichever of gold or silver serves the poor better. Today that is silver, the lower threshold. Darul Ifta Birmingham advises silver and counts either as valid.
Others use gold, holding that silver has fallen far in value against gold since nisab was set, and that the gold figure is nearer the other nisab thresholds.

notes.sourceLead: Mukhtasar al-Quduri, Book of Zakat, on valuing goods for sale by whichever of gold or silver serves the poor better; Darul Ifta Birmingham, answer on the nisab threshold for gold; IslamOnline fiqh, answer on what the nisab of money is measured by, for the gold view

evidence.place: Book of Zakat, chapter on trade goods
evidence.quote: يقومها بما هو أنفع للفقراء والمساكين منهما

notes.text: This calculator adds all your assets together by value and compares the total with one nisab.

positions.text: Gold, silver and goods for sale are added together to reach nisab.
Gold and silver are added together to reach nisab.
Gold is not added to silver, nor silver to gold; each needs its own nisab.
Gold or silver you hold is added to the value of your goods for sale to reach nisab.

notes.sourceLead: Mukhtasar al-Quduri, Book of Zakat, chapter on trade goods; al-Risala of Ibn Abi Zayd, chapter on zakat of money; 'Umdat al-Fiqh, Book of Zakat, chapter on trade goods; Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Book of Zakat, on adding gold to silver. Matn Abi Shuja' does not address it, so the Shafi'i position rests on Fath al-Mu'in and Ibn Rushd's report

evidence.quote: ويجمع الذهب والفضة في الزكاة فمن كان له مائة درهم وعشرة دنانير فليخرج من كل مال ربع عشره

evidence.place: Chapter on zakat
evidence.quote: ولا يكمل أحد النقدين بالآخر

notes.text: Gold and silver kept as savings, coins or bars count in every school. Jewellery that is worn is where they differ.

positions.text: Zakat is due on gold and silver jewellery, whether it is worn or not.
No zakat is due on jewellery kept for permitted wear. In the Shafi'i school this is the relied-upon view. In the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, jewellery kept only as savings counts.

notes.text: Debts you owe are where the schools differ on what to take off before comparing with nisab.

positions.text: A debt that covers all your wealth means no zakat is due. If you have more than you owe, zakat is due on what is left when it reaches nisab.
Debts are taken off cash, gold and silver, but they are first set against belongings you own that carry no zakat, when those can cover them.
A debt that covers your nisab, or takes you below it, means no zakat is due.
In the school's relied-upon view, debts are not taken off. Zakat is due on the wealth you hold.

notes.sourceLead: Mukhtasar al-Quduri, Book of Zakat; al-Risala of Ibn Abi Zayd, chapter on zakat of money; 'Umdat al-Fiqh, Book of Zakat, chapter on debt; for the Shafi'i school, al-Nawawi's Minhaj al-Talibin, Book of Zakat, and Kifayat al-Akhyar, since Matn Abi Shuja' does not address it; Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Book of Zakat

notes.text: Goods you hold to sell are counted at what they would sell for on the day your zakat year completes. The Maliki school treats a trader who holds goods for a long time, waiting for a price, differently from one who buys and sells all the time. For your own situation, ask a scholar you trust.
notes.sourceLead: Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Book of Zakat, section on trade goods; al-Risala of Ibn Abi Zayd, chapter on zakat of money; Matn Abi Shuja' and 'Umdat al-Fiqh, Book of Zakat

notes.text: This calculator counts money owed to you that you expect to be repaid. The schools differ on when its zakat is paid, each year or once it is repaid, and on whether it is then paid for every year that passed or for one. For your own situation, ask a scholar you trust.

notes.text: The zakat year is a lunar year, counted from the day your wealth first reached nisab.
notes.sourceLead: Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ijma', Book of Zakat; Ibn Rushd, Bidayat al-Mujtahid, Book of Zakat, who reports the jurists' agreement and says no hadith on it is firmly established. The report "no zakat on wealth until a year passes over it" is in Abu Dawud, from Ali, and Ibn Majah, from Aisha, Book of Zakat. Ibn Hazm, al-Muhalla, on the year being twelve months by the new moons

notes.text: If your wealth drops below nisab during the year, the schools differ on whether the year starts again. The Maliki position is not shown: we could not confirm it in the school's primer.

positions.text: What counts is having nisab at the start and the end of the year. A dip in between does not restart it.
Gold and silver must be at nisab for the whole year. Goods for sale are measured at the end of the year only, in the school's relied-upon view.
Goods for sale must be worth nisab for the whole year.
